subject: WSJ Economics: Just How Moderate Are ‘Moderate’ Democrats?

96 Plus, change at the CBO, Russia’s oil resilience and one reason more young people are gambling   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Greg Ip   Just How Moderate Are ‘Moderate’ Democrats?   Plus, change at the CBO, Russia’s oil resilience and one reason more young people are gambling   Moderates delivered Democrats’ midterm majorities. Naturally they think they, not the progressive acolytes of senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, ought to set the party’s agenda.

   But what agenda? The “moderate” label is slapped on a range of candidates, some of whose positions wouldn’t sound moderate to the median voter.

   This became apparent at last week’s summit in Denver of Majority Democrats, an umbrella group that promotes centrist candidates .

   The group’s chair, Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss, delivered an address that would warm a supply-sider’s heart. Democrats, he said, need to let go of bad ideas, “most urgently the ones that ignore supply and demand. Supply and demand is a reality, and the fact is when supply goes down, prices go up.” He argued in favor of natural gas and nuclear power to lower utility prices, and against rent control and exclusionary zoning, which make housing expensive.

   Yet there was James Talarico, Texas’s senator-elect, calling for “universal healthcare” in his speech at the conference by allowing anyone to buy into Medicare. Former transportation secretary and Denver headliner Pete Buttigieg ran for president in 2020 on a similar proposal. This would entail a costly expansion of government-funded healthcare. It appears that anything short of Medicare-for-all now qualifies as moderate.

   Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a progressive turned moderate, wants sectoral wage bargaining, double pay for overtime and a “New Deal-style public jobs program.” Former President Joe Biden governed to the left of Bill Clinton and Barack Obama and didn’t go that far.

   Where these Democrats have truly moderated is on immigration, climate and culture. They talk about a secure border, not transgender rights, and promise to meet voters where they are. As Gallego likes to say: “Every Latino man wants a big-ass truck.”  

   Moving toward the center on culture seems to have eased the way to moving left on economics. Gina Hinojosa, a progressive member of the Texas Legislature who wasn’t in Denver, captured the Texas governor’s mansion by avoiding cultural issues. The Washington Post reports that she plans to govern as a moderate . Among her plans: freezing electricity rates, a data-center moratorium and $1,500 checks to everyone. Not your father’s moderation.

   Read my column on Rahm Emanuel, former mayor of Chicago, radical centrist and possible Democratic presidential candidate. 

   This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter , your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics.   If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       What I’m Following   Democrats will name Congress’s next budget watchdog at an anxious moment for the fiscal outlook. Phillip Swagel, director of the Congressional Budget Office, is leaving the agency when his term ends in January. My colleague Richard Rubin tells me: “Swagel, who has run CBO since 2019, is returning to his pre-CBO post at the University of Maryland. He has drawn praise from lawmakers in both parties but sometimes some spirited criticism, particularly from Republicans who say CBO is too pessimistic on forecasting policy-driven economic growth. Democrats will pick Swagel’s replacement, choosing the CBO head for the first time since 2009. That decision will likely be led by Sen. Tim Kaine (D., Va.), who is in line to become chairman of the Senate Budget Committee.”

   Refinery strikes aren’t crippling Russia : Ukrainian drone strikes have taken out a reported 30% to 59% of Russian refining capacity. “If those figures reflected real output losses, Russia would face a catastrophic fuel shortage. Yet we do not see this ,” Sergey Aleksashenko, a former Russian deputy finance minister, writes. He estimates 40% of strikes between April 1 and Sept. 25 had no impact on sales volume, and only 10% resulted in stoppages lasting three or more weeks. Half of Russian diesel is exported, so diesel capacity affects Russians less than gasoline, where shortages have eased since the summer. The strikes “have hurt Russia but have not yet altered its capacity to wage war.”

   Young people are more likely to gamble when long-run financial goals seem out of reach. In South Korea, young people who won a lottery for the right to buy price-regulated apartments cut back on their use of crypto-trading apps by 21%, Yale’s Costas Arkolakis and four co-authors found in a new report. On the other hand, among people who recently lost a job, crypto trading rose by 6%. The research suggests that young people are drawn to the YOLO (“you only live once”) economy of crypto, prediction markets and meme stocks when they don’t see a clear path to financial milestones.

       More From WSJ         • “ The cost pressure is everywhere ,” Kraft Heinz Chief Executive Steve Cahillane says. More food inflation is on the way, from snarled supply chains, unpredictable weather and, increasingly, high fuel prices. 

   • What China’s intelligence apparatus has historically lacked in sophistication, it makes up for in scale . China-backed hackers outnumber all of the FBI’s cyber personnel at least 50 to 1, according to a 2023 FBI assessment. 

   • Nvidia’s days as an open checkbook for the AI economy are numbered. The downfall of Jensen Huang means the AI ecosystem may lose one of its most profligate sources of funding .

       What to Watch   Tuesday 

   • 8:30 a.m. ET: Economists expect to see that retail sales grew by 0.2% last month, including 0.4% growth in the “control group” categories that feed into GDP numbers.

   • 9:15 a.m. ET: Forecasters think that U.S. industrial production likely increased by just 0.1% in October, cooling from a 0.7% increase in September.

   Wednesday 

   • 2 a.m. ET: Stubborn inflation isn’t just America’s problem. Analysts are expecting to see that U.K. inflation ticked up to 3.6% last month, versus 3.5% a month earlier. Core inflation likely held steady at an elevated 2.8%.

   • 2:30 p.m. ET: Hot inflation data has prompted a renewed conversation about whether the Fed might accelerate coming interest-rate increases. New York Fed President John Williams, speaking at a Manhattan event, may weigh in on how the Fed will proceed in December and beyond.

       You Have Thoughts   Last Thursday in this section , we misspelled the name of reader Joseph Somervell. 

   In that same newsletter, we told you about the proposal—from a research group led by former Biden economic adviser Lael Brainard—to offer federally insured mortgages to first-time home buyers with low $1,000 down payments. South Carolina reader Woody Rash writes (edited for length and clarity): 

   What could go wrong with only a $1,000 down payment on a government-insured mortgage? Has she forgotten the mortgage debacle of 2005-2007 and the subsequent near collapse of the economy known as the great financial crisis? This is a disaster waiting to re-occur. During that period, I witnessed firsthand how all the policies promoting mortgages of low quality laid low firms such as Merrill Lynch, Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers.

   Thoughts on what you just read? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me at wsjeconomics@wsj.com . Include your state (or country) to be considered for publication. 

       What I’m Reading   • A range of data suggest the elderly’s incomes are falling relative to those of working-age people, the young are accumulating more wealth and governments are introducing more policies that benefit the young. ( The Economist )

   • Populist nationalism has triumphed this decade at the ballot box. But liberal individualism still rules popular culture and has done more to shape how people really live, Janan Ganesh writes. ( Financial Times )

   • Experts fear that flying has become more dangerous under President Trump, James Fallows writes. One piece of evidence: a rise in dangerous runway incursions since 2024. ( New York Times Magazine )

       About Me   I’m The Wall Street Journal’s chief economics commentator. I’ve been writing about economics, markets and politics for more than 40 years, in the U.S. and from around the world.

Just How Moderate Are ‘Moderate’ Democrats?
 
Plus, change at the CBO, Russia’s oil resilience and one reason more young people are gambling
 

Moderates delivered Democrats’ midterm majorities. Naturally they think they, not the progressive acolytes of senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, ought to set the party’s agenda.

 

But what agenda? The “moderate” label is slapped on a range of candidates, some of whose positions wouldn’t sound moderate to the median voter.

 

This became apparent at last week’s summit in Denver of Majority Democrats, an umbrella group that promotes centrist candidates.

 

The group’s chair, Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss, delivered an address that would warm a supply-sider’s heart. Democrats, he said, need to let go of bad ideas, “most urgently the ones that ignore supply and demand. Supply and demand is a reality, and the fact is when supply goes down, prices go up.” He argued in favor of natural gas and nuclear power to lower utility prices, and against rent control and exclusionary zoning, which make housing expensive.

 

Yet there was James Talarico, Texas’s senator-elect, calling for “universal healthcare” in his speech at the conference by allowing anyone to buy into Medicare. Former transportation secretary and Denver headliner Pete Buttigieg ran for president in 2020 on a similar proposal. This would entail a costly expansion of government-funded healthcare. It appears that anything short of Medicare-for-all now qualifies as moderate.

 

Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a progressive turned moderate, wants sectoral wage bargaining, double pay for overtime and a “New Deal-style public jobs program.” Former President Joe Biden governed to the left of Bill Clinton and Barack Obama and didn’t go that far.

 

Where these Democrats have truly moderated is on immigration, climate and culture. They talk about a secure border, not transgender rights, and promise to meet voters where they are. As Gallego likes to say: “Every Latino man wants a big-ass truck.”  

 

Moving toward the center on culture seems to have eased the way to moving left on economics. Gina Hinojosa, a progressive member of the Texas Legislature who wasn’t in Denver, captured the Texas governor’s mansion by avoiding cultural issues. The Washington Post reports that she plans to govern as a moderate. Among her plans: freezing electricity rates, a data-center moratorium and $1,500 checks to everyone. Not your father’s moderation.

 

Read my column on Rahm Emanuel, former mayor of Chicago, radical centrist and possible Democratic presidential candidate.

 

This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter, your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What I’m Following

 

Democrats will name Congress’s next budget watchdog at an anxious moment for the fiscal outlook. Phillip Swagel, director of the Congressional Budget Office, is leaving the agency when his term ends in January. My colleague Richard Rubin tells me: “Swagel, who has run CBO since 2019, is returning to his pre-CBO post at the University of Maryland. He has drawn praise from lawmakers in both parties but sometimes some spirited criticism, particularly from Republicans who say CBO is too pessimistic on forecasting policy-driven economic growth. Democrats will pick Swagel’s replacement, choosing the CBO head for the first time since 2009. That decision will likely be led by Sen. Tim Kaine (D., Va.), who is in line to become chairman of the Senate Budget Committee.”

 

Refinery strikes aren’t crippling Russia: Ukrainian drone strikes have taken out a reported 30% to 59% of Russian refining capacity. “If those figures reflected real output losses, Russia would face a catastrophic fuel shortage. Yet we do not see this,” Sergey Aleksashenko, a former Russian deputy finance minister, writes. He estimates 40% of strikes between April 1 and Sept. 25 had no impact on sales volume, and only 10% resulted in stoppages lasting three or more weeks. Half of Russian diesel is exported, so diesel capacity affects Russians less than gasoline, where shortages have eased since the summer. The strikes “have hurt Russia but have not yet altered its capacity to wage war.”

 

Young people are more likely to gamble when long-run financial goals seem out of reach. In South Korea, young people who won a lottery for the right to buy price-regulated apartments cut back on their use of crypto-trading apps by 21%, Yale’s Costas Arkolakis and four co-authors found in a new report. On the other hand, among people who recently lost a job, crypto trading rose by 6%. The research suggests that young people are drawn to the YOLO (“you only live once”) economy of crypto, prediction markets and meme stocks when they don’t see a clear path to financial milestones.

 
 
 

More From WSJ

 
 
 
 

• “The cost pressure is everywhere,” Kraft Heinz Chief Executive Steve Cahillane says. More food inflation is on the way, from snarled supply chains, unpredictable weather and, increasingly, high fuel prices. 

 

• What China’s intelligence apparatus has historically lacked in sophistication, it makes up for in scale. China-backed hackers outnumber all of the FBI’s cyber personnel at least 50 to 1, according to a 2023 FBI assessment. 

 

• Nvidia’s days as an open checkbook for the AI economy are numbered. The downfall of Jensen Huang means the AI ecosystem may lose one of its most profligate sources of funding.

 
 
 

What to Watch

 

Tuesday

 

• 8:30 a.m. ET: Economists expect to see that retail sales grew by 0.2% last month, including 0.4% growth in the “control group” categories that feed into GDP numbers.

 

• 9:15 a.m. ET: Forecasters think that U.S. industrial production likely increased by just 0.1% in October, cooling from a 0.7% increase in September.

 

Wednesday

 

• 2 a.m. ET: Stubborn inflation isn’t just America’s problem. Analysts are expecting to see that U.K. inflation ticked up to 3.6% last month, versus 3.5% a month earlier. Core inflation likely held steady at an elevated 2.8%.

 

• 2:30 p.m. ET: Hot inflation data has prompted a renewed conversation about whether the Fed might accelerate coming interest-rate increases. New York Fed President John Williams, speaking at a Manhattan event, may weigh in on how the Fed will proceed in December and beyond.

 
 
 

You Have Thoughts

 

Last Thursday in this section, we misspelled the name of reader Joseph Somervell.

 

In that same newsletter, we told you about the proposal—from a research group led by former Biden economic adviser Lael Brainard—to offer federally insured mortgages to first-time home buyers with low $1,000 down payments. South Carolina reader Woody Rash writes (edited for length and clarity):

 

What could go wrong with only a $1,000 down payment on a government-insured mortgage? Has she forgotten the mortgage debacle of 2005-2007 and the subsequent near collapse of the economy known as the great financial crisis? This is a disaster waiting to re-occur. During that period, I witnessed firsthand how all the policies promoting mortgages of low quality laid low firms such as Merrill Lynch, Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers.

What I’m Reading

• Populist nationalism has triumphed this decade at the ballot box. But liberal individualism still rules popular culture and has done more to shape how people really live, Janan Ganesh writes. (Financial Times)
